summary: A deep-sea hunter with fangs too long for its mouth and a row of light organs it uses to become invisible from below.
discovery: First formally described in the scientific literature.

physical.label: Fangs
physical.value: So long they close outside the jaw, beside the eyes

physical.label: Photophores
physical.value: Rows of light organs providing counter-illumination camouflage

physical.label: Spine
physical.value: The first vertebra absorbs shock from ramming prey

diet_notes: Migrates upward 1,500 m every night to feed, then returns to the depths before dawn.

behavior.label: Vertical migration
behavior.value: Part of the largest daily animal migration on Earth

behavior.label: Hunting
behavior.value: Rams prey at speed, impaling it on the fangs

behavior.label: Metabolism
behavior.value: Can survive 12 hours between meals only by moving very little

how_to_help: Support habitat protection, avoid wildlife products and report sightings to citizen-science platforms.
facts: Its fangs are so long they would pierce its own brain if the jaw closed normally.
It joins a nightly vertical migration of billions of animals.
Photophores on its belly erase its silhouette from below.
It can go weeks without food.

summary: The blue star lotus of ponds and tank-lakes — national flower of Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, often confused with the true lotus.
discovery: First formally described in the scientific literature.

physical.label: Leaves
physical.value: Float flat on the surface with a notch to the centre

physical.label: Flowers
physical.value: Float or sit just above water, unlike lotus which stands tall

physical.label: Roots
physical.value: Anchored in pond mud with long flexible stalks

reproduction.label: Flowering
reproduction.value: Opens in the morning, closes by afternoon for 3 days

reproduction.label: Seeds
reproduction.value: Released underwater and dispersed by fish and birds

behavior.label: Day blooming
behavior.value: Tracks the sun's schedule precisely

behavior.label: Shelter
behavior.value: Pads shade water, reducing algae and sheltering fish

behavior.label: Distinction
behavior.value: Lotus leaves are peltate and emergent; lily pads float and are notched

how_to_help: Support habitat protection, avoid wildlife products and report sightings to citizen-science platforms.
facts: It is the national flower of Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.
Water lilies float; lotus flowers stand above the water on stalks.
The Amazon giant water lily can support a small child on its 3 m pads.
Monet painted around 250 water lily canvases at Giverny.

summary: Ants that build living nests by pulling leaves together and stitching them with silk squeezed from their own larvae.
discovery: First formally described in the scientific literature.

physical.label: Mandibles
physical.value: Strong enough to hold body chains bridging gaps

physical.label: Larval silk
physical.value: Adults use larvae as living glue guns

physical.label: Strength
physical.value: Can lift 100 times its own weight

reproduction.label: Colony
reproduction.value: Up to 500,000 ants across dozens of nests in many trees

behavior.label: Nest building
behavior.value: Chains of ants pull leaves together while others 'sew' with larval silk

behavior.label: Biological control
behavior.value: Used in Asian orchards for 1,700 years — the oldest recorded pest control

behavior.label: Territory
behavior.value: Aggressively excludes other insects from its trees

conservation_notes: Chinese citrus growers were placing weaver ant nests in orchards by 304 CE — the earliest documented biological pest control.
how_to_help: Support habitat protection, avoid wildlife products and report sightings to citizen-science platforms.
facts: Weaver ants use their own larvae as glue guns.
They form living chains to bridge gaps between leaves.
A single colony can span 20 trees.
Their nests and larvae are eaten as a delicacy across Southeast Asia.

summary: The most economically important insect on Earth — a superorganism of 50,000 individuals that communicates food locations through a symbolic dance.
discovery: Described by Linnaeus in 1758; domesticated for at least 9,000 years.

physical.label: Wings
physical.value: Beat 230 times per second, producing the familiar buzz

physical.label: Eyes
physical.value: Two compound eyes of 6,900 facets plus three simple ocelli

physical.label: Corbicula
physical.value: Pollen baskets on the hind legs

physical.label: Sting
physical.value: Barbed in workers, so it tears free and kills the bee

physical.label: Vision
physical.value: Sees ultraviolet nectar guides invisible to humans

diet_notes: A colony gathers nectar from about 2 million flowers to make 500 g of honey, flying the equivalent of twice around the Earth.
food_chain: Primary pollinator — underpins roughly a third of global food production
lifespan_notes: Summer workers live 6 weeks, winter workers 5 months, and a queen 3–5 years.

reproduction.label: Queen
reproduction.value: Lays up to 2,000 eggs a day

reproduction.label: Mating flight
reproduction.value: Mates with 10–20 drones once, storing sperm for life

reproduction.label: Castes
reproduction.value: Fertilised eggs become workers or queens; unfertilised become drones

reproduction.label: Royal jelly
reproduction.value: Diet alone determines whether a larva becomes a queen

lifecycle.detail: 3 days
6 days of rapid feeding
12 days in a capped cell
Progresses through nurse, builder, guard and forager roles

behavior.label: Waggle dance
behavior.value: Encodes direction relative to the sun and distance to food — a true symbolic language

behavior.label: Thermoregulation
behavior.value: Workers shiver or fan to hold the brood nest at 35 °C

behavior.label: Swarming
behavior.value: The old queen leaves with half the colony to found a new one

behavior.label: Democracy
behavior.value: Scout bees 'vote' on a new nest site through dance intensity

conservation_notes: One in three mouthfuls of human food depends on pollinators. India's Apis cerana indica and stingless Tetragonula bees are equally vital and far less studied.
how_to_help: Plant native flowering species, avoid systemic pesticides, buy from local beekeepers and leave shallow water dishes in summer.
facts: Bees communicate the location of flowers through the waggle dance — decoded by Karl von Frisch, who won a Nobel Prize for it.
A worker bee produces about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her entire life.
Honey never spoils — edible honey has been found in 3,000-year-old Egyptian tombs.
Bees see ultraviolet patterns on flowers that are invisible to us.
A colony flies about 90,000 km to produce a single kilogram of honey.
Queens can lay more than their own body weight in eggs every day.
Bees recognise individual human faces in laboratory tests.

subspecies.name: Giant rock bee
subspecies.note: Apis dorsata laboriosa, makes hallucinogenic 'mad honey'

summary: The largest fish alive — a gentle, spotted filter feeder the length of a bus, revered by Gujarati fishermen as 'Vhali', the daughter of the sea.
discovery: First formally described in the scientific literature.

physical.label: Mouth
physical.value: 1.5 m wide with 300+ rows of vestigial teeth it never uses

physical.label: Spots
physical.value: A unique constellation pattern used like a fingerprint by researchers

physical.label: Skin
physical.value: Up to 15 cm thick — the thickest of any animal

physical.label: Gills
physical.value: Filter pads strain plankton from 6,000 litres of water an hour

diet_notes: Feeds by ram filtration and active suction, sometimes hanging vertically to gulp dense plankton clouds.
migration: Individuals tracked over 20,000 km across the Pacific.

behavior.label: Temperament
behavior.value: Completely harmless to humans; divers swim alongside

behavior.label: Aggregations
behavior.value: Hundreds gather at seasonal plankton blooms

behavior.label: Diving
behavior.value: Descends below 1,900 m

conservation_notes: India gave the whale shark full Schedule I protection in 2001 — the first such listing in Asia — after a Gujarat campaign led by religious leaders transformed hunters into protectors.
how_to_help: Support habitat protection, avoid wildlife products and report sightings to citizen-science platforms.
facts: Whale sharks are fish, not whales, and are completely harmless.
Each one has a unique spot pattern, catalogued with astronomy software.
They filter 6,000 litres of water every hour.
Gujarat's fishermen call them Vhali — 'the dear one'.
They may live 80–130 years.

summary: An Ice Age elephant insulated by a metre of hair and 10 cm of fat, which survived on Wrangel Island until 4,000 years ago — after the pyramids were built.
discovery: First formally described in the scientific literature.
population: Last population died out around 1650 BCE

physical.label: Coat
physical.value: An outer layer of guard hairs up to 90 cm over dense underwool

physical.label: Tusks
physical.value: Curved, up to 4.2 m long

physical.label: Ears
physical.value: Small to reduce heat loss and frostbite

physical.label: Fat
physical.value: A 10 cm insulating layer plus a shoulder hump

diet_notes: Ate up to 180 kg of mammoth-steppe vegetation a day, using tusks to sweep snow aside.

reproduction.label: Calves
reproduction.value: One at a time, protected by the matriarchal herd

behavior.label: Herds
behavior.value: Matriarchal family groups like modern elephants

behavior.label: Coexistence
behavior.value: Hunted by humans and depicted in cave art at Rouffignac and Chauvet

behavior.label: Extinction
behavior.value: Warming climate plus human hunting fragmented and finished them

threats: Habitat collapse of the mammoth steppe
conservation_notes: Frozen mammoths preserved in permafrost have yielded complete genomes, and several companies are attempting de-extinction by editing Asian elephant DNA.
how_to_help: Support habitat protection, avoid wildlife products and report sightings to citizen-science platforms.
facts: Mammoths were still alive when the Great Pyramid of Giza was built.
Their DNA has been sequenced from permafrost carcasses.
Baby mammoth Lyuba, found in Siberia, is 42,000 years old and almost perfectly preserved.
They had small ears to prevent frostbite, unlike African elephants.
Their closest living relative is the Asian elephant.
